chunks: From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali Al-Hashimi, from Muhammad ibn Isa, who said: Muhammad ibn Abi Umair narrated to us from Zayd al-Rassi, who narrated to us from Ubayd ibn Zurarah, who said: I heard Zurarah asking Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the fasting of the day of Ashura.

He (peace be upon him) said: Whoever fasts it, his portion from fasting that day is the portion of Ibn Marjanah and the family of Ziyad. I said: And what is their portion from that day? He said: The Fire (Hell).

The way to reconcile these narrations is what our Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) used to say: Whoever fasts the day of Ashura on the path of grief due to the calamity of the family of Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the distress over what befell his progeny, he has succeeded. And whoever fasts it based on what our opponents believe regarding the virtue of its fasting, seeking blessings in it, and believing in its barakah and happiness, he has sinned and erred.

key_terms.آلِ زِيَادٍ: The family of Ziyad, governors of Basra/Kufa associated with the Umayyads
key_terms.ابْنُ مَرْجَانَةَ: Ibn Marjanah, a companion of Imam Ali known for fasting Ashura out of joy/victory
key_terms.الْحُزْنِ: Grief, specifically regarding the calamity of the Prophet's family
key_terms.عَاشُورَاءَ: Ashura, the 10th day of the month of Muharram

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between fasting Ashura for Shia and non-Shia intentions?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Istibsar* highlights the Shia jurisprudential nuance of *I'tibar* (consideration of intention) regarding the fasting of Ashura. While the narration warns against the 'Hellfire' associated with those who view it as a day of inherent blessing (like the pagan Ibn Marjanah), Sheikh al-Tusi reconciles this by distinguishing between fasting out of grief for the Ahl al-Bayt, which is rewarded, and fasting out of mere tradition or belief in its sanctity, which is considered erroneous.
